region.en: Cliff above the up-river trail, Nez Perce country (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 內茲珀斯故地上行小道旁峭壁（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by Herbert J. Spinden, 1907; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Nez Perce Tales, 1. Coyote's Wars' (Mountain-Sheep Girl)

summary.en: A girl at the top of a cliff calls Coyote to come finish killing a mountain-sheep for her; as he looks over the edge she catches his neck with her forked stick and pushes him over, throwing the body into the river when she finds her victim is only Coyote. Magpie pecks his eyes awake — 'You were in no battle; you were pushed over the cliff and killed by Mountain-Sheep Girl' — and tells him how to even the score. Going up a second time, Coyote asks to take the stick and be shown where to stand; as she shows him, he catches her with the forked stick, pushes her over the cliff, and kills her.
summary.zh: 崖頂少女呼郊狼代其射殺大角羊；郊狼俯崖張望之際，她以分叉木杖鉤其頸推落。見死者竟是郊狼，棄屍河中。喜鵲啄其目使醒——『爾未曾征戰，乃為大角羊女推落崖下』——並授以報復之策。郊狼二度上山，反求持杖並請其指示站位；少女俯身指點之際，郊狼持杖鉤之，推落懸崖，反殺其人。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Nez Perce narrative collected by Spinden (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote was travelling up the river. He heard some one calling to him from far off: a woman's voice said to him, 'Come here and finish killing him for me!' He looked, and saw a girl standing at the top of a cliff. She had a bow and arrows, but could not use them, and she was trying to kill Mountain-Sheep; so Coyote went up to help her. Besides the bow and arrows, she had a forked stick. She asked Coyote to look over the cliff and see how best they could get at Mountain-Sheep; and while he was doing this, she caught his neck with the forked stick and pushed him over the cliff. Then she went down where he had landed; and when she saw that her victim was only Coyote, she threw the body into the river.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 180 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Coyote floated down the river a bend and a half, and stranded. Magpie came flying up the river, and when he saw Coyote he thought to himself, 'I wonder if there is matter in his eyes!' When Magpie began pecking at the eyes of Coyote, however, the latter came to, and said to Magpie, 'Why are you flying around here? I myself have just been to battle, capturing women.' Magpie replied, 'You were in no battle; you were pushed over the cliff and killed by Mountain-Sheep Girl.' Then Magpie told Coyote what to do to play even.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 180 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: So Coyote travelled upstream a second time, and again he heard her call. He went up to her; and when she asked him to do the same thing, he replied, 'Now, let me take the stick, and then you show me just where I have to stand in order to see Mountain-Sheep plainly.' When she went to show him, Coyote caught her with the forked stick, pushed her over the cliff, and killed her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 180 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.

region.en: Riverbank trysting-place, Nez Perce country (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 內茲珀斯故地河畔相會處（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by Herbert J. Spinden, 1907; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Nez Perce Tales, 1. Coyote's Wars' (Mussel-Shell Woman)

summary.en: A woman by the river calls Coyote to come and lie with her; in the embrace she kills him, and throws the body into the water when she sees it is only Coyote. Magpie, feeding on his eyes, wakes him — 'No, you were over there with Mussel-Shell Woman, who cut off your penis and killed you' — and teaches the counter-trick. Coyote goes up the river a third time, and at the same place the woman calls to him again; but now Coyote has a bone which he uses instead, so he kills her, saying, 'You will be only a mussel-shell, and Indians will eat you, but you will not be able to hurt any one.'
summary.zh: 河畔婦人呼郊狼前來相就；相擁之間，郊狼被其陰所傷而斃。婦見死者不過郊狼，棄屍入水。喜鵲啄目使醒——『爾非征戰，乃為蚌殼女所殺』——並教以破解之法。郊狼三度前往，其地婦人又呼；此番郊狼以獸骨代身，反殺其人：『爾從此只是蚌殼，印第安人將食爾，然不能再傷人。』

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Nez Perce narrative collected by Spinden (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Sexual motif summarized plainly as recorded. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Then Coyote resumed his journey up river; and by and by he heard another woman, who called to him to come and lie with her. He arrived where the woman was; then he embraced her. His organ was cut off, and he died. When the woman saw that it was only Coyote she had killed, she threw the body into the water, and it drifted down the river.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 180 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Again Magpie saw the body, and came to feed on the matter in the eyes. Coyote came to, and said, 'Why did you wake me up? I have been to war, capturing women.' Then Magpie answered, 'No, you were over there with Mussel-Shell Woman, who killed you.' So again Magpie told him what to do to kill her in turn. He went up the river, and at the same place the woman called to him again; but now Coyote had a bone which he used instead of his member. So he killed her, and said, 'You will be only a mussel-shell, and Indians will eat you, but you will not be able to hurt any one.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 180-181 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: The Bungling Host: Coyote and his Four Sons-in-Law
title.zh: 笨拙之主：郊狼與四女婿

region.en: Winter camps of the Nez Perce, ice-holes on the river (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 內茲珀斯冬季營地，河上冰洞（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by Herbert J. Spinden, 1907; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Nez Perce Tales, 2. The Bungling Host'

summary.en: Visiting Elk, Mountain-Sheep, Otter and Fish-Hawk in turn, Coyote watches each son-in-law's magic — a bent green stick cooked in ashes becoming elk marrow-gut, excrement becoming camas, a piece of his wife's dress boiled into mountain-sheep meat, five thorn sticks through five ice-holes strung with fish, a dive from a leaning tree bringing up salmon-trout — and attempts every one at home: the withhe burns and the stick straightens, killing his wife (whom he brings back to life); only blood comes when he tries Elk's trick; his wife's dress stays elk-skin; diving under the ice he drifts to the rapids, nearly drowned, until Otter rescues him and fills all five sticks himself; and diving head-first from the tree, Coyote misses the hole and breaks his head against the ice — coming to only to find his visitor gone.
summary.zh: 郊狼依次拜訪麋、大角羊、水獺、魚鷹四位女婿，暗記其魔法：彎枝燼埋即成麋骨髓腸；穢物化卡瑪斯根；割妻裙入釜即成羊脂美肉；五荊枝穿五冰洞，枝枝掛魚；自斜樹俯衝冰洞，滿載鱒鮭。返家一一效仿：藤燃枝直，火燄四射，擊斃其妻（復活之）；仿麋術，唯得鮮血；仿羊術，裙仍為皮；潛冰逐流，漂至急灘，幾乎滅頂，賴水獺相救並代為滿掛五枝；自樹頭俯衝，失準撞冰，昏死——醒時賓客已散。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Nez Perce narrative collected by Spinden (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: One of Coyote's daughters had married an Elk, one a Mountain-Sheep, one an Otter, and one a Fish-Hawk; moreover, Coyote had a little boy. 'My son, let us go and see your oldest sister to-morrow!' said Coyote in the evening. When Coyote got to the house, they went in and sat there for a while. Soon Coyote saw Elk step outside to cut off a stick about as big as an arm and as long as two arms. Elk brought the stick into the tent and built a big fire; then Coyote saw the green stick roasting in the fire. Soon Elk took the stick out, turned the ends together so that it formed a hoop, dug a hole in the ashes and buried the bent stick. Pretty soon the stick was cooked; and when Elk took it out, it had turned into the marrow gut of an elk.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 181 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Elk gave Coyote a flint knife and told him to begin eating. 'Well, I never eat stick,' said Coyote to himself, so he gave the knife to his boy; but soon Coyote turned his head and saw the boy eating the stick, and it seemed so very rich that he took it away from him. When they had eaten as much as they could, they had used up only half. After this meal Elk asked for a winnowing-basket, went outside with the basket and knife, and Coyote ran to the door and peeked out through a hole: he saw Elk squat over the basket and stick the knife up his anus. When Elk brought in the basket and set it down, Coyote would not eat, because he had seen how Elk had obtained this food; so he gave it to the boy, saying he would eat after nobody. When the boy liked the food, however, Coyote also began to eat: it was camas.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 181 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Before leaving Elk's camp, Coyote told Elk to be sure and return the visit the next day. Next morning Elk dressed himself up and went over; Coyote jumped up and ran outside to look for a good green stick, brought it in, built up a big fire, bent the hot stick and tied the ends together with a withe, dug a hole in the ashes and buried the stick. When the withe burnt through, the stick straightened out and threw the fire out of the fireplace and all over the tent; Coyote's wife was sitting near the door, and the stick hit her in the back and killed her. Coyote brought his wife back to life, and told his boy to get him a winnowing-basket; he stepped outside to do as Elk had done, stuck his knife up his anus, but all he could get was blood. Coyote could not produce his guest's dinner by magic; so Elk took pity on him, cut a stick as before, put it into the fire, telling Coyote to take it out when it was done, and also filled up the basket.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 181-182 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: That night Coyote said to his boy, 'We will go and see the next oldest girl.' They set out next morning. Mountain-Sheep heated water in a willow basket; his wife was sitting with her back to the fire, and Mountain-Sheep took hold of her dress and cut away a piece of it at the back, and put this piece into the cooking-basket. Coyote shut his eyes; and when he opened them, the dress of the woman was whole again. When the food was cooked, Coyote thought, 'I do not care at all about eating my daughter's dress' — but when the boy started to eat it, Coyote saw that it was the very best mountain-sheep meat, so he ate it too. The next morning Mountain-Sheep went to Coyote's camp, where Coyote heated rocks, sharpened his flint knife, caught his wife by the back of the dress and cut the dress away as far down as the waist — 'You crazy old woman! I must have some meat for my son-in-law' — cut up the back of the dress in small pieces and put them into the boiling water, but what he took out was nothing but elk-skin. When Mountain-Sheep saw that Coyote was trying to imitate him, he pulled off his shirt and cut away all below the waist, telling Coyote to boil this; the shirt-tails came back on Mountain-Sheep's shirt.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 182 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Coyote then visited Otter, who had five holes cut in the ice in a row near the middle of the river: laying down four sticks beside the farthest hole, he dove into the river with one stick, and when he came up, the stick was all strung with fish — five times, once at each hole, a string of fish each time. Coyote got up very early and cut five holes in the ice, got five good thorn switches, ran down to the last hole, laid down four of the sticks, and dove into the river with one of them; he drifted downstream under the ice and got no fish, drifting down to the rapids, and then came out almost drowned. Otter rescued Coyote and took him home; then he dove down as before and came up with the sticks full of fish. After a day or so, Coyote visited Fish-Hawk, whose camp had a dead tree leaning over the river and five small holes cut in the ice just under it: Fish-Hawk flew out of the house, circled around in the air, alighted on the tree, flew off, and dove for the lowest hole, coming back with a whole string of salmon-trout, two more strings of salmon-trout, and two strings of suckers. Coyote went home, cut five holes under a leaning tree, took the switches down to the river, climbed the tree, looked around a bit, and dove down head-first — he missed the hole, and broke his head against the ice. After a while Coyote came to; when he came to, he found that his visitor had gone.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 183-184 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Coyote and Fox Get Food: The Deer-Tick Man

region.en: Camp door where the five packs fall (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 五袋食物墜落之營門（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by Herbert J. Spinden, 1907; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Nez Perce Tales, 4. Coyote and Fox get Food'

summary.en: Coyote, the wise one, and Fox, the slow-witted, need food; Coyote wishes aloud — 'I wish that I and my friend could hear the sound of five packs of food falling at the door!' — and five sounds answer, tlitluk five times. He takes the three largest packs (all dry meat without fat) for himself and leaves the two smallest (fine rich meat) for Fox, then takes Fox's second pack too, accusing him of not dividing with a friend. Five times the magic act repeats; the sixth time Coyote cuts a peep-hole to see who brings the meat, and sees a man with long hair in a wig going up over the ridge — Deer-Tick. 'Oh, you man with the wig! you go over the mountain!' he shouts after him — and, the chorus asks, did they ever get food again from the man Coyote had shamed? No.
summary.zh: 智者郊狼與拙者狐斷糧。郊狼許願：『願吾與友得聞門前五袋食物落地之聲！』五聲『咕咚』應之。郊狼自取三大袋（皆無脂之乾肉），留二小袋（精美肥肉）與狐；翌日又取狐之第二袋，反怪其『不分與友』。如此五次皆驗；第六次，郊狼鑿窺孔欲見送肉者，見一戴假髮之長髮男子越脊而去——乃鹿蝨翁。郊狼追呼：『戴假髮的傢伙，滾過山去！』自辱恩人，肉源遂絕。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Nez Perce narrative collected by Spinden (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote was a wise man, and Fox was slow-witted. Coyote said to Fox, 'Now we shall have to get up some scheme to procure food. You are slow-witted, just like your father. My father was not that way: he was wise. I have taken after my father.' They were in their camp; and Coyote said to Fox, 'If you keep perfectly still and do not move, we shall get some food.' Then Coyote began thus: 'I wish that I and my friend could hear the sound of five packs of food falling at the door!' Then they heard five sounds: 'tlitluk, tlitluk, tlitluk, tlitluk, tlitluk!' Coyote jumped up and ran out, and there he saw five packs lying at the door. He took the three largest ones for his share, and left the two smallest ones for Fox.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 184 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: The large packs that Coyote got were all dry meat without any fat, but the two little packs contained fine meat. In three days Coyote had eaten all his poor meat, while Fox had a great deal left, because his was so very rich. On the fourth morning Coyote was hungry, and kept his eye on Fox to see if he had eaten all his share; Fox had eaten only one of his packs, so Coyote jumped over and took the other. Then he said to Fox, 'You are a fine fellow never to divide up with your friend!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 184-185 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Five times they repeated the magic act and got food, but the sixth time Coyote wanted to see who brought them the meat. Fox replied, 'You had better not try to do that, because this is the only way we can get food.' But Coyote was determined to see: he stood at the door and cut a peep-hole so that he could look out with one eye. Then he repeated the wish; and when the packs fell, he saw a man going up over the ridge who wore long hair in a wig. This man was Deer-Tick. Coyote shouted after him, 'Oh, you man with the wig! you go over the mountain!' Think you they got food again from the man Coyote had shamed? No.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 185 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.

region.en: Race-course of gulches and hills ending in a steep hill (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 越溝跨嶺、末段陡坡之賽道（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by Herbert J. Spinden, 1907; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Nez Perce Tales, 5. Coyote and Fox run Races'

summary.en: The Mountain-Sheep, Elk, Black-Tailed Deer, White-Tailed Deer and Mountain-Goat outran all other animals, the wager being that the beaten should lose their heads. Coyote and Fox challenge five Black-Tailed Deer: Coyote gives out half-way, Fox finishes and wins, the five deer are beheaded in a gulch, and the two devour the bodies; they beat the other four kinds the same way, until no animal dares race them. Then Jack-Rabbit, White Mountain-Rabbit, Bald-Headed Eagle, Golden Eagle and Magpie challenge the fattened pair; Coyote gives out, all the other side gives out but Magpie, who swoops down at the last steep hill and wins. Coyote asks only for a drink before his head is cut off, strips, crawls into the water under a root — 'Here is Coyote! He is crawling under the root!' cry the playing children — and they pull him out and behead both. It did Coyote no good to hide after he had lost.
summary.zh: 大角羊、麋、黑尾鹿、白尾鹿與山羊五族跑遍天下無敵，賭注為敗者斬首。郊狼與狐挑戰五頭黑尾鹿：半途郊狼力竭，狐竟完賽得勝，五鹿於溝中斬首，二人食其屍。此後連敗四族，無獸敢應。待其食肥，野兔、白毛兔、白頭鵰、金鵰、喜鵲聯手挑戰；郊狼又敗，對方亦皆力竭，唯喜鵲末段俯衝奪魁。郊狼求飲水再受刑，卻脫衣潛入水下樹根——戲童高呼：『郊狼在此！鑽入樹根下！』眾童拖出二人，一併斬首。敗後藏匿，終屬徒勞。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Nez Perce narrative collected by Spinden (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: The Mountain-Sheep, the Elk, the Black-Tailed Deer, the White-Tailed Deer, and the Mountain-Goat outran all other animals; the wager was that those who were beaten should lose their heads. These five animals always won. Now, Coyote and Fox happened to come to that place; and Coyote said to Fox, 'Partner, we also shall give them a race, we two against those five.' They made a challenge, and arranged a race with five Black-Tailed Deer; so they ran a long way, crossing gulches and hills, but when the race was about half over, Coyote gave out, and Fox was left to finish. Pretty soon the five Black-Tailed Deer gave out also, and so Fox won the race. Then the five Black-Tailed Deer were beheaded in a gulch, and Coyote and Fox devoured the bodies and rested. After this, Coyote and Fox ran races with each of the other four kinds of animals; they won all the races, and killed the defeated runners.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 185 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: No other animals dared to run with Coyote and Fox. Soon, however, these two got fat from eating too much meat; then Jack-Rabbit and White Mountain-Rabbit, and Bald-Headed Eagle, and Golden Eagle, and Magpie decided to challenge them. Coyote said to Fox, 'We have beaten all the good runners; let us beat these as well!' The race was a long one, as before; and Coyote gave out, and every one on the other side gave out but Magpie. Magpie was behind Fox when they came to a steep hill at the end of the course; then Magpie swooped down and won the race.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 185-186 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Coyote said to the victors, 'You are fine runners, and have beaten us fairly. Just let me get a drink of water, and then you may cut off my head.' So they told him to get a drink and come back. Now, down at the creek there were some children playing, and they saw Coyote take off his clothes and crawl into the water and under a root. A boy cried out, 'Here is Coyote! Come on! He is crawling under the root!' They all pulled him out and took him where Fox was, and then they beheaded both. It did Coyote no good to hide after he had lost.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 186 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.

region.en: Sick-lodges of the Nez Perce villages (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 內茲珀斯村落病帳（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by Herbert J. Spinden, 1907; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Nez Perce Tales, 6. Fox and Coyote as Shamans'

summary.en: Several persons suffering from swellings of the body sent for Fox to treat them and make the swelling go away; when these persons were nearly well, Coyote asked Fox for permission to help in the curing — Fox let Coyote act as shaman, and the patients grew worse again. This happened several times: Fox would make them better, and Coyote would turn round and make them worse. By and by the sick ones ordered Fox to tell Coyote not to help, because he was not a good medicine-man.
summary.zh: 村中多人身患腫疾，請狐醫治。病者將癒之際，郊狼請求協助施術；狐允之，病人病情復惡。如此數番：狐使之好轉，郊狼一出手又使之惡化。病者終於下令：不許郊狼再插手——蓋其醫術拙劣，不足為薩滿。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Nez Perce narrative collected by Spinden (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Spinden notes the story illustrates the custom of dismissing medicine-men who could not effect cures. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Now, there were several persons suffering from swellings of the body, and they sent for Fox to treat them and make the swelling go away. When these persons were nearly well, Coyote asked Fox for permission to help in the curing. So Fox let Coyote act as shaman, and the patients grew worse again. This happened several times: Fox would make them better, and Coyote would turn round and make them worse. By and by the sick ones ordered Fox to tell Coyote not to help, because he was not a good medicine-man.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 186 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Coyote and the Moon: The Nez Perce Version
title.zh: 郊狼與月神：內茲珀斯版本

region.en: Watch-point on the hill above Moon's camp (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 月神營地山頭瞭望點（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by Herbert J. Spinden, 1907; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Nez Perce Tales, 7. Coyote and the Moon'

summary.en: Moon's son sits on the point of a hill watching the up-river trail, killing people and taking the bodies home to his father, who eats the private parts raw and cooks the rest. Coyote creeps close with a hat of grass, greets the startled watcher as 'nephew,' conjures the pile of stones where 'our fathers kept watch' and a spring of very good water, asks to hold the club while Moon-Youth drinks — and kills him with it. He exchanges clothes, carries the body home, and the old Moon eats and notices the difference — 'This meat is almost too strong' — while Coyote pretends illness. Three nights Coyote steals away with his belongings and three times wakes just outside the doorway, having travelled nowhere; then he kills the old Moon: 'After this you will kill no longer, but will give light for travel at night-time; and now and then men of importance will know Coyote's moon.' And thus it happened.
summary.zh: 月神之子常踞山頭守望上行小道，誅人後負屍歸家；其父生食其私，熟食其餘。郊狼以草帽掩形潛近，驚呼『賢姪！』，幻出『先父曾共守之』的石堆與甘泉，借其棒一擊斃之。易服負屍歸家，老月神食而覺異——『此肉太烈』——郊狼佯病不食。三夜三度携物潛逃，三度醒於門口，寸步未移。郊狼恐事敗露，終殺老月神：『從此爾不得殺人，只為夜行者照路；重要人物偶爾得見「郊狼之月」。』事遂如此。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Nez Perce narrative collected by Spinden (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Parallel version of the Moon-slaying (cf. Sahaptin record). Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Moon had a son who used to sit on the point of a hill and watch the up-river trail that passed near their camp. The son used to kill people and take the bodies home to his father, who cooked and ate them; but the private parts he ate first, and without cooking. This happened for many years, and Coyote learned of it. And Coyote came towards that place; and, behold! there was that one far off on the hill, watching for people. Coyote kept out of sight, and made himself a hat of grass; whenever the Moon-Youth turned his head, Coyote would creep closer, and then lie flat on his belly and be very still. In that manner he went very close to him; and right by his side he took off the hat and spoke to Moon-Youth, saying, 'Halloo, nephew! this is the wrong place for you to sit and watch.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 186 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: And the Moon-Youth jumped with fright, thinking, 'I wonder whence he came towards me!' And Coyote said, 'Your father and mine used to keep watch over there, where that little pile of stones is, whenever it was cold. Many they killed, and nobody ever took them unawares.' And, sure enough, the pile of stones was there, and they built a fire. Then again Coyote spoke: 'We are thirsty, but yonder is a spring of very good water; let us get a drink!' They went there, and, sure enough, Moon-Youth found the spring. Coyote said, 'Now, drink!' but Moon-Youth had his club in his hand; so Coyote said, 'Let me hold it for you!' and he gave the club to Coyote, and leaned over to drink from the spring. Then Coyote struck Moon-Youth with the club and killed him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 187 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: He exchanged clothes with that one, and carried the body up to the house. The old Moon heard the falling load, and cried out, 'Son, bring him in!' And then Moon took out his knife and cut off the private parts and ate them. And he noticed a difference, and he said, 'This meat is almost too strong'; but he cooked the rest of the body, and offered some of the flesh to Coyote, who pretended to be ill, and ate nothing. Then it came evening, and they lay down to sleep; Coyote collected his belongings, and stole away from the old man. He travelled till it was nearly morning, and then said to himself, 'It is getting daylight; I will go to sleep, or else I shall be too sleepy for the day.' Then Moon arose from his bed, and saw him sleeping there just by the doorway of the house: 'How is this? you must have had a nightmare during the night.' And it surprised Coyote: 'I thought I had travelled a great distance,' he said to himself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 187 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: And again it was growing dark, and again Coyote set out, and assured himself that he had indeed travelled a long way; but he was only just outside the doorway of the house. And again Moon arose, and found him sleeping right there, but did not recognize him as Coyote rather than his son. Thus it was for three times; and then Coyote decided to kill Moon, for fear the latter would soon see the difference. So Coyote killed him, and said, 'After this you will kill no longer, but will give light for travel at night-time; and now and then men of importance will know Coyote's moon.' And thus it happened.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 187 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Frog and Coyote: The Widow who Stopped the River

region.en: Fountain-head of the river, source lodge (symbolic pin)

texts.period: Collected by Herbert J. Spinden, 1907; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Nez Perce Tales, 8. Frog and Coyote'

summary.en: A widow, Frog, maltreated and angry, goes up the river to the source and sits over the fountain-head, so that the entire river goes dry except in some deep holes. Coyote travels up the dry bed making five rafts placed about five bends apart, finds her lodge, drinks her bucket dry, watches through an eye-hole in his blanket as she refills it from the ground she sits on, sets tule rushes to give war-whoops — but the Frog widow will not budge. So Coyote seizes her by the arm and jerks her up; the water comes out, and when it is running freely he throws her into the stream: 'This is the way you will always be: whenever high water comes, it will always carry frogs down the river.' Running downstream, he finds the first four rafts broken adrift and jumps aboard the fifth just as it breaks loose.
summary.zh: 寡婦蛙受辱懷憤，行至河源，坐鎮泉眼之上，全河為之斷流，唯深潭有水。郊狼沿乾河床上行，沿途每五個河灣置一木筏。至源頭之廬，飲盡其桶中水；於毯上留一窺孔，見她自坐處地下汲水。郊狼命香蒲草代為吶喊助威——蛙寡婦仍不為所動。郊狼遂執其臂猛提，水乃湧出；待河水暢流，將她擲入河中：『爾將永遠如此：每當春汛暴漲，蛙必隨流而下。』郊狼狂奔而下，前四筏皆已被沖散，第五筏方散之際，他一躍而上，順流而歸。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Nez Perce narrative collected by Spinden (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: There was a widow, Frog, who was maltreated and became angry. So she went up the river to the source, and sat over the fountain-head, so that the entire river went dry: there was no water except in some deep holes. Now, the people had not missed her; but Coyote thought something like this must have happened to make the river go dry. He went upstream, because he knew the place where the water had been stopped. As he travelled up the dry bed, he made five rafts, and placed them about five bends of the river apart.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 187 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: At the head of the river he saw a lodge. He was nearly dead of thirst when he arrived; so he entered the lodge. Inside he saw a mountain-sheep-horn bucket of water, and he said to the woman, 'Pass that water over to me; I have drunk a great deal of water along the river to-day, still I am very dry.' So he drank up all the water. Coyote lay down on the opposite side of the lodge from the woman, and covered his head with his blanket; but he had an eye-hole in the blanket, and he saw her rise, take the empty bucket, and dip up water from where she had been sitting. After this, Coyote arose and went out.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 187 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Near that place he spat upon some tule rushes, and told them to give war-whoops after he had re-entered the lodge. So he went again into the lodge, and soon there was a great noise of war-whoops. He said out loud to himself, 'I thought I heard something when I was outside.' But for all his strategy, the Frog widow would not budge from where she sat. So Coyote seized her by the arm and jerked her up; then the water came out. When the water was running freely, he threw the woman into the stream, saying, 'This is the way you will always be: whenever high water comes, it will always carry frogs down the river.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 188 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Coyote then started downstream, running as fast as he could. When he reached the place of the first raft, he found it had broken adrift; so he ran on to the next one, and found it also adrift, and the third the same, and the fourth. He reached the fifth, however, just as it was breaking loose, and managed to jump aboard. Then he went down the river on the raft. This is how Coyote recovered the water from Frog.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 188 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Grizzly-Bear the Chief and the Poisoned Arrows

region.en: Draw between the hills of the great hunt (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 大狩獵之山間谷地（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by Herbert J. Spinden, 1907; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Nez Perce Tales, 9. Grizzly-Bear and Coyote'

summary.en: Coyote, jealous of Grizzly-Bear the chief, declares a great hunt and stations six of his friends — each with an arrow poisoned with rattlesnake-poison — in Grizzly-Bear's rich draw, telling the chief, 'If you see objects like men, do not be afraid, for they are only rocks.' Grizzly-Bear goes up close and is shot; skinned and cooked, his meat is served at Coyote's feast, where his sister and wife know by the smell and weep in silence. The two women plan to kill the hunters one by one, but a Black-Bear in camp tells Coyote, so the hunters go out in bands of three and four; when Grizzly-Bear's wife is killed, that put an end to it all. A younger brother and the sister were spared, so that there would always be grizzly bears in the country.
summary.zh: 郊狼妒忌酋長灰熊，詐稱大狩獵，遣六名親信各携響尾蛇毒箭埋伏於灰熊必經之富谷，並囑酋長：『見似人之物勿懼，乃石耳。』灰熊近前，中箭而死。剝皮烹肉，郊狼設盛宴分食；灰熊之妻與妹聞其味而知，暗自垂淚，懼郊狼而不敢言。二女謀逐一誅殺獵人，然營中黑熊告密；郊狼遂令獵人三五成群而行。灰熊之妻被誅，事乃終。其幼弟與妹得免，故世間灰熊至今不絕。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Nez Perce narrative collected by Spinden (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Grizzly-Bear was a chief, and Coyote was jealous of him. Now, Coyote had many friends who would do whatever he told them to do. He arose early in the morning, and announced that there would be a great hunt that day, and that he himself would take part in it; so the people all went out, and with them went Grizzly-Bear.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 188 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Coyote told his friends just what to do when they arrived at the hunting-grounds. He told the people that he wanted Grizzly-Bear to go up a draw between the hills, because he was a chief and the best hunting was there, and every one could scare the game towards him. He told all the people where to hunt, and he stationed six of his friends in the hunting-ground of Grizzly-Bear; Coyote had some arrows poisoned with rattlesnake-poison, and gave one arrow to each of his friends. These men waited for Grizzly-Bear with their arrows on their bows.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 188-189 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Coyote said to Grizzly-Bear, 'If you see objects like men, do not be afraid, for they are only rocks.' When Grizzly-Bear saw the men, he was afraid; but Coyote shouted to him, 'Do not be at all afraid!' Grizzly-Bear went up close to the men, and they shot him with their arrows. When he was dead, they skinned him and took him into camp; the sister and wife of Grizzly-Bear were in this camp along with the six hunters. When Coyote came into camp, he went around and made a speech to all the people, bidding them to a great feast when the game they had taken was cooked. Soon the meat was cooked and dressed up finely; then every one was called in to the feast, and the sister and wife of Grizzly-Bear were called in with the rest. As soon as they entered, they knew from the smell that the meat was Grizzly-Bear meat; the tears rolled from their eyes, but they were afraid of Coyote, and said nothing.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 189 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: The wife and sister made up their minds to get revenge; their plan was to go with the hunters and kill them one by one. But there was a Black-Bear in camp who heard the planning of the two women, and told Coyote; as a result of this, Coyote did not send out the hunters one by one, but in bands of three and four. When the wife of Grizzly-Bear was killed, that put an end to it all. A younger brother and the sister were spared, so that there would always be grizzly bears in the country. That is the reason there are still grizzly bears.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 189 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Coyote of the Lower Country: The Buffalo-Horn Cure

region.en: Abandoned camp of the buffalo country (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 野牛之鄉棄營（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by Herbert J. Spinden, 1907; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Nez Perce Tales, 12. Coyote of the Lower Country'

summary.en: Riding to the buffalo country in his war-bonnet, Coyote finds a deserted camp with one tent left, inside it a young girl whom the people left behind — really the Mountain-Sheep girl, with a buffalo-horn run into her foot, swelled so badly that her relatives abandoned her. She asks the medicine-man to cure her, agreeing to marry him in payment, and Coyote sings his cure-song — 'I will bite and pull it out' — pulls out the horn with his teeth, pounds roots and leaves onto the wound, and in a few days the girl is well and marries him. In the main camp another Coyote makes a speech about the cured girl — not liking the affair at all; that night his own wife elopes with another. 'Well, I feel pretty badly. Still the thing cannot be helped. Others will feel as badly as I when they go to the Buffalo country and their wives run away from them.' Sadly he went back to his former home, and since that time wives have often run away from their husbands in the Buffalo country.
summary.zh: 郊狼冠戰盔赴野牛之鄉。至一廢營，僅餘一帳，帳中有一被族人遺棄之少女——實為大角羊女，足中被野牛角刺入，腫痛難行。她求醫並允以婚姻為酬。郊狼唱咒歌『吾咬而拔之』，以齒銜角拔出，敷以搗碎之草根樹葉；數日而癒，遂成夫婦，隨營而行。大營中另一郊狼演說其事，心實不悅；當夜其妻私奔他人。郊狼哀曰：『吾心甚悲，然事已如此。後人赴野牛之鄉而妻逃者，必同此感。』從此野牛之地，婦人棄夫而逃者，時有所聞。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Nez Perce narrative collected by Spinden (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Coyote made up his mind one morning that he would go to the Buffalo country too. So he started; he was ready for war, and had on his war-bonnet. After a while he came to where there had been a big camp; he went all around the camp-site, and found that one tent remained, and in it he heard some one groaning. So Coyote went into this tent. He saw there a young girl whom the people had left behind; she was really the Mountain-Sheep girl. She had run a buffalo-horn into her foot, and it had swelled so badly that her relatives had been forced to abandon her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 191 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: When Coyote first entered the tent, the girl recognized him as a medicine-man. So she said to him, 'The people have all gone off and left me. I wish you would cure me. If I get well, I will pay you for it.' Coyote said, 'What if your parents refuse to pay me? If I cure you, I want you to marry me in payment.' The girl agreed to this, so he began to treat her. He sang a song: 'I will bite and pull it out, I will bite and pull it out.' The horn was projecting just enough to offer a hold for his teeth; so Coyote took hold of it in this way, and easily pulled it out. Coyote gathered some roots and leaves, and pounded them up and put them on the wound; in a few days the girl was well. Then she married Coyote, and they followed up the camps till they came upon the rest of the people.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 191-192 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: In that camp there was another Coyote, who made a speech to the people, relating how the girl that had been left behind was in camp again after having been cured by a strange Coyote; in reality, this affair was not to the liking of the Coyote who made the speech. While the strange Coyote and his wife were staying at the camp, preparations were under way to send out a war-party, and singing was taking place; so this Coyote told his wife that he too was going to war, but for her to continue with him until camp was broken. That night, however, she did not come back to him: she had eloped with another. Coyote felt very badly over this, and said, 'Well, I feel pretty badly. Still the thing cannot be helped. Others will feel as badly as I when they go to the Buffalo country and their wives run away from them.' Sadly he went back to his former home, and since that time wives have often run away from their husbands in the Buffalo country.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 192 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.

region.en: Imnaha River timber, robber-owl's home ground (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 伊姆納哈河畔林間，鴞魔橫行之地（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by Herbert J. Spinden, 1907; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Nez Perce Tales, 13. The Owl-Monster'

summary.en: A mother refused water by her children sticks her husband's feathers along her arms and flies out of the smoke-hole, becoming a raven; the father turns himself into an old flint-lock gun. The orphaned children take the trail to their grandfather, but the Owl-Monster (Palxhotske, 'robber' — a timber owl living on the Imnaha River who called to persons from afar) sees them; they turn up moss, crawl under it and become grubs, but are picked into her pack-bag. Changing their voices, they shout, 'The Imnaha widow's children are on fire!' and become heavy to carry; the tired monster hangs the bag on a limb and hurries home, and the children kick the bag to pieces and run for their grandfather's river. He first denies them — 'I have no grand-children except those whose mother has become a raven and whose father has become a flint-lock gun' — then recognizes them, stretches his leg across the river, and hides them under the canoe he is hewing. When the Owl-Monster demands passage, he has Butterfly, Crawfish, Mussel, Bullhead and Swallow ferry her in a canoe of wild-parsnip, telling her the boat will run steady if she ties rocks around her neck and body; about the middle of the river Crawfish splits the canoe, and the Owl-Monster went to the bottom and was drowned.
summary.zh: 母親索水不得，縛鷹羽於臂，自煙囪飛出，化為渡鴉；其父化為老式燧發槍。孤兒兄妹啟程投奔祖父，途中為鴞魔 Palxhotske（意為『強盜』，棲於伊姆納哈河之林鴞，慣於遠處呼人）所見。兄妹掀苔蘚鑽入其下化為幼蟲，仍被拾入背囊。二人變聲遙呼：『伊姆納哈寡婦的孩子著火啦！』又自變沉重；鴞魔力竭，掛囊於樹梢奔家探視；兄妹踢破囊袋而遁。祖父初不肯認——『吾孫唯鴉母槍父之子孫』——後認出，伸腿為橋渡之，藏於所鑿獨木舟下。鴞魔索渡，祖父遣蝶、螯蝦、蚌、鯰、燕以野防風草舟渡之，誘其頸身繫石以穩舟；至中流，螯蝦裂舟，鴞魔沉底溺斃。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Nez Perce narrative collected by Spinden (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Variant of the Owl cycle (cf. Sahaptin record). Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: The man used to go hunting, and the woman used to go digging for roots. They had two children, a boy and a girl. The woman came home in the evening tired out and thirsty; and she asked the children to fetch her some water, but they refused to go for it. Now, her husband had left some feathers hanging to a lodge-pole. She told the children she would become a raven if they did not fetch her water, but still they refused to go; so she stuck the feathers along her arms, and flew out of the smoke-hole of the lodge.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 192 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the man came home, he asked the children where their mother was. At first they did not like to tell him, but after a while they decided to tell him the truth. He scolded them, and said, 'You are wicked children, and I do not wish to live with you any longer.' So he turned himself into an old flint-lock gun. Now, these children had often heard their father talk about their grandfather, who lived not far away; they left their home and took the trail. On the way an Owl-Monster (Palxhotske) saw them. When they were aware that the Owl-Monster had seen them, they turned up a piece of moss, crawled under it, and became grubs. Then the Owl-Monster searched for them, and finally found the two grubs; he put them into his pack-bag, and carried them off upon his back.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 192-193 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: The little girl said to the little boy, 'Let us try something!' So they changed their voices, and shouted from afar off. They called out, 'The Imnaha widow's children are on fire!' Then they changed themselves into real persons, and were heavy to carry. Pretty soon the Owl-Monster grew very tired, and she stopped and hung up the bag upon the limb of a tree; she wanted to get home at once to her children. When she was out of sight, the children kicked the bag to pieces, and obtained their freedom; then they ran as fast as they could toward the place where their father had told them their grandfather lived. When they came to the side of the river opposite his lodge, they called out for him to come over and rescue them from a monster that pursued them. The first time he paid no attention to their cries; and the second time he told them that he had no grand-children except those whose mother had become a raven, and whose father had become a flint-lock gun.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 193 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the Owl-Monster found that her children were safe, she hastened back to her bag, and learned that the children had escaped; she tracked them down towards the river. But when the Owl-Monster was almost there, the grandfather recognized his grand-children, stretched his leg out across the river, and then drew it back with the children upon it; he hid them under a canoe he was hewing out. Then the Owl-Monster came to the river-bank and shouted to be taken across. The old man grew tired; so he asked Butterfly, Crawfish, Mussel, Bullhead, and Swallow to go over and get the Owl-Monster. They had a canoe made of wild-parsnip. When they asked her to step in, the boat was so unsteady that she was afraid, and stepped out again; so they told her the canoe would run steady if she tied rocks around her neck and body. She did this, and when she stepped aboard, the canoe was very steady. They pushed off; and about the middle of the river, Crawfish split the canoe, and the Owl-Monster went to the bottom and was drowned.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 194 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Frog and Bluejay: The Climbing Race on the Smooth Pole
title.zh: 蛙與冠藍鴉：光滑木柱攀爬賽

region.en: Smooth pole set in the ground of the animal village (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 獸村中之光滑木柱（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by Herbert J. Spinden, 1907; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Nez Perce Tales, 14. Frog and Bluejay'

summary.en: Frog had a smooth pole set in the ground and with it devised a means of killing off all the birds: a race up the pole, whoever got to the top first cutting off the other's head. The pole leaned a little, and Frog would take the upper side and make the opponent take the under side — so Frog went on winning races and killing off many birds. Coyote, afraid Frog would kill off all the birds, gave a big feast to work out a plan; every one was afraid to race her, until Bluejay undertook the job. Half way up Frog tried to kick Bluejay off the pole; near the top Bluejay used his wings and flew the rest of the way, got to the top first, kicked her, and she fell to the ground and was killed — which is why there are no feathers on the side of Bluejay's face. Coyote made a speech: 'Hereafter there will be frogs on the earth, but they will never hurt any one. People will hear the frogs singing, and then they will know that warm weather is coming.'
summary.zh: 蛙立一光滑木柱，藉以誅殺群鳥：賽者攀柱而上，先至頂者斬對方之頭。柱身微傾，蛙必居上坡而令對手居下坡——由是連戰連勝，鳥類死傷慘重。郊狼恐鳥類滅絕，設宴共謀；眾皆不敢應戰，冠藍鴉自告奮勇。攀至半途，蛙欲踢其墜；將近頂端，冠藍鴉展翅飛登，先至而踢之——蛙墜地而死。故冠藍鴉至今面頰無羽——蛙當年攀扯所致。郊狼演說曰：『從此蛙將存於世，但不害人。人聞蛙鳴，便知暖春將至。』

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Nez Perce narrative collected by Spinden (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Frog had a smooth pole set in the ground, and with it he had devised a means of killing off all the birds: a race would be run up this pole, and whoever got to the top first would cut off the other one's head. The pole leaned a little; and Frog would get on the upper side, and make the opponent get on the under side. Thus Frog continued to win races for a long time, and managed to kill off many birds.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 194 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Coyote was in this camp. He became afraid that Frog was going to kill off all the birds. So Coyote gave a big feast, and invited every one to attend; he wanted the people to work out a plan to get the best of Frog, but every one was afraid to run him a race. After a scheme had been devised, Bluejay undertook the job; and Coyote made a speech, calling everybody to the pole, and announcing that there was to be a race between Frog and Bluejay.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 194 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Now, little Frog became uneasy, and feared that Bluejay was going to win and then kill her. So when they were half way to the top, Frog tried to kick Bluejay off the pole; when they were nearly to the top, Bluejay used his wings and flew the rest of the way. He got to the top first. When Frog got to the top, Bluejay kicked her, and she fell to the ground and was killed. Ever since that race there have been no feathers on the side of Bluejay's face, because Frog had torn them all off when she tried to knock Bluejay from the pole. After the race was over, Coyote made a speech, saying, 'Hereafter there will be frogs on the earth, but they will never hurt any one. People will hear the frogs singing, and then they will know that warm weather is coming.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 194 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: The Diving Beaver and the Mud-Hen's Trick

region.en: Riverbank of the diving contest (symbolic pin)

texts.period: Collected by Herbert J. Spinden, 1907; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Nez Perce Tales, 15. The Diving Beaver'

summary.en: Beaver had a plan to kill off all animals that could dive: a test of staying under water till one or the other was dead. Just after daylight Otter and Beaver had a diving-test; the rest of the people sat on the bank and watched, and when it was almost evening Otter floated up dead, and Beaver came up alive. Beaver kept up these tests and killed off different animals, until soon all were afraid of him and none would dive with him. Coyote called the people together to make up a plan to kill Beaver at his own game: Mountain-Woodpecker was to bore a hole in the bottom of a canoe on the river, and Mud-Hen was to stick her head out of this hole where no one could see her. So Beaver and Mud-Hen dove, Mountain-Woodpecker sat over the hole and pulled out the plug, Mud-Hen put her head out through it and went to sleep; just before dark there was a stream of bubbles, and Beaver came up dead. Mountain-Woodpecker woke Mud-Hen: 'Beaver has come up dead; now you would better dive down and come up in the middle of the river' — and Mud-Hen dove down and came up again some distance from the canoe.
summary.zh: 河貍欲誅盡善潛之獸，立比試之規：閉氣水下，孰先斃命。天方破曉，水獺與河貍較藝，眾人岸觀；至傍晚，水獺浮屍而起，河貍活著現身。河貍連連設局，誅戮不同水獸；眾皆懼之，無人敢與比試。郊狼召集族人共謀：啄木鳥在河上獨木舟底鑽孔，泥鷸自孔中探首而匿。賽時，河貍與泥鷸同潛；啄木鳥拔去孔塞，泥鷸探首而眠。日落前夕，水中氣泡連串，河貍浮屍而出。啄木鳥喚醒泥鷸：『河貍已死，快潛往河心浮起！』泥鷸潛下，於距舟甚遠處現身。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Nez Perce narrative collected by Spinden (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Beaver had a plan to kill off all animals that could dive. This plan was to have a test of staying under water till one or the other was dead. Just after daylight Otter and Beaver had a diving-test; the rest of the people sat on the bank and watched. When it was almost evening, Otter floated up dead; after this, Beaver came up alive. So Beaver kept up these tests, and killed off different animals. Soon all were afraid of Beaver, and none would dive with him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 194 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Coyote called the people together, and asked them to make up a plan to kill Beaver at his own game. The Mud-Hen said, 'Let us try once more!' Now, Mud-Hen had made a plan with Mountain-Woodpecker: Mountain-Woodpecker was to bore a hole in the bottom of a canoe that was on the river, and Mud-Hen was to stick her head out of this hole where no one could see her. So Beaver and Mud-Hen dove, and Mountain-Woodpecker sat over the hole in the canoe and pulled out the plug; Mud-Hen put her head out through this hole and went to sleep. Just before dark there was a stream of bubbles, and then Beaver came up dead. Pretty soon Mountain-Woodpecker woke up Mud-Hen, and said, 'Beaver has come up dead: now you would better dive down and come up in the middle of the river.' So Mud-Hen dove down, and came up again some distance from the canoe.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 195 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: The Sun and the Moon: Frog on His Eye

region.en: Council of the people beneath the too-hot sun (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 烈日下族人聚議（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by Herbert J. Spinden, 1907; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Nez Perce Tales, 16. The Sun and the Moon'

summary.en: The Sun had two wives, Frog and another woman; then the Sun moved across the sky so very hot that the people were nearly killed by the heat, and they did not like this state of affairs. Coyote called a council of all the people; and he knew Sun did not love Frog and would not invite her to come, so he begged her to come to the council and obey what Sun told her to do. She went and stood at the door and said, 'My husband, where am I to sit?' and he told her, 'Here, on my eye.' Then she advanced a few steps and jumped up to his eye, and the people tried to pull her off, but could not. Coyote told the Sun, 'You are acting badly for a chief,' and decided that Sun should become the night sun (Moon) and that the Moon should become the Sun: the irregular one is now the Moon, and the frog is seen over his eye.
summary.zh: 太陽有二妻：蛙與另一女。其後太陽越行越烈，幾將世人烤斃。郊狼召集全族大會；知太陽不寵蛙妻、必不召其前來，遂請蛙妻赴會並聽從太陽吩咐。蛙妻立於門前問：『夫君，吾當坐於何處？』太陽答：『此處，坐吾眼上。』蛙妻即躍上其目；眾人拉之不下。郊狼斥曰：『身為酋長，豈能如此無狀！』遂判定：烈日者貶為夜日（月），夜日者升為太陽。故今日之月即昔日乖戾之太陽，蛙影仍懸其目。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Nez Perce narrative collected by Spinden (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: The Sun had two wives, Frog and another woman. Then the Sun moved across the sky so very hot, that the people were nearly killed by the heat; they did not like this state of affairs. For that reason Coyote called a council of all the people; and he knew Sun did not love Frog, and would not invite her to come, so he begged her to come to the council and obey what Sun told her to do.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 195 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: So she went and stood at the door, and said, 'My husband, where am I to sit?' and he told her, 'Here, on my eye.' Then she advanced a few steps and jumped up to his eye; and the people tried to pull her off, but could not. And Coyote told the Sun, 'You are acting badly for a chief'; and Coyote decided that Sun should become the night sun (Moon), and that the Moon should become the Sun. So the irregular one is now the Moon, and the frog is seen over his eye.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 196 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Wildcat: The Old Chief's Cure and the Fog
title.zh: 野貓酋長：淨身除疾與迷霧

region.en: Abandoned camp of the animal village (symbolic pin)

texts.period: Collected by Herbert J. Spinden, 1907; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Nez Perce Tales, 17. Wildcat'

summary.en: In a large village of animals there was an old Wildcat with the itch, scratching himself all the time with his walking-stick; a girl of the same lodge picked it up now and then to scratch herself with, and, still doing it after being told not to, found herself pregnant and gave birth to a child. Coyote made a speech advising the people to move camp and abandon old-man Wildcat, the girl and the baby — so they did. Wildcat would never leave the house but lay with his head covered; it had been foggy ever since. Taking pity on the girl, he had her dig him a bathing-hole, hot-stoned it, bathed in the hot water and then in the stream, the scabs falling from his body: he became a fine young man, hunted two deer the same evening, and every morning after they had all the food they could eat. Magpie, thinking of the girl, found the camp thriving, was invited back with his family, and told; Coyote made another speech — 'Magpie has been back to our old camp, where we abandoned those persons. They have plenty of meat there' — the people moved back, Wildcat never allowed it to be foggy any more, and he became the head chief of the village.
summary.zh: 獸村中有一老野貓，遍體疥瘡，終日以杖搔癢；同帳少女偶取其杖自搔，雖經制止仍犯，竟而懷孕產子。郊狼提議遷營，棄老野貓、少女與嬰兒於原地——眾從之。野貓蒙首而臥，自那時起山中常起迷霧。野貓憐其女，令其掘一浴坑，燒石入水；晨浴熱湯，繼入寒溪，疥痂盡脫，化為英挺青年。當晚即獵得二鹿，此後每日晨獵，衣食無缺。喜鵲憶起此女，探營見其興旺，被邀舉家遷回；郊狼又演說——『喜鵲已回我等廢棄之舊營，彼處食物豐足』——族人重返。野貓從此不再起霧，且成為村中首席。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Nez Perce narrative collected by Spinden (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: There was a large village of animals, and in this village there was an old Wildcat. He had the itch, and was scratching himself all the time; he had a walking-stick that he used in scratching his back. Now, there was a girl in the same lodge as Wildcat, and now and then she would pick up his cane and scratch herself with it. He told her not to do this; and when she still did it, she found that she was pregnant. Soon she gave birth to a child. Coyote then made a speech concerning this girl and her baby, advising the people to move camp and abandon old-man Wildcat, the girl, and the baby; so the people abandoned them, and moved to another place.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 195 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Wildcat would never leave the house, but would lie about with his head covered up; they had nothing to eat. After a while Wildcat took pity on the girl. He told her to dig for him a hole in the ground outside of the camp, where he could bathe; she did this, and filled the hole with water, and then put stones on a fire and heated them, and then put the hot stones into the water. Early in the morning she carried Wildcat down to the bathing-place and left him. After Wildcat had bathed in the hot water, he walked down to the stream and bathed in cold water; when he washed himself, the scabs fell from his body, and he became a young man. He called to the girl to bring his clothes; and when he put them on, he was a fine young man. Along toward evening, he took his bow and arrow and began to hunt: he killed two deer. Every morning after that he hunted, and they had all the food they could eat; the baby grew fast.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 195-196 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: About a month later, Magpie happened to think of this girl. He said to himself, 'I will go and see if they are dead.' When Magpie saw the camp, he wondered what new person had come there; the baby was playing with some deer-tallow outside the lodge. When Magpie alighted and began to eat the tallow, the baby cried, and the woman came out and invited Magpie to enter; she gave him food to eat there, and more to take home. The woman said to Magpie, 'Get your belongings and come back to-night and live with us, but do not tell any one except your own family.' Now, it had been foggy ever since Wildcat uncovered his head, after being abandoned by the people; Magpie waited until dark before going into camp, then he gave the meat to his wife and children. Some people looked in at the door, and saw the Magpies eating a meal, while every one else was hungry; after this, he told them where he had obtained his meat. Then Coyote made another speech, saying, 'Magpie has been back to our old camp, where we abandoned those persons. They have plenty of meat there.' Next morning he made another speech: 'Everybody get together their belongings, and we will move back to the place where Wildcat lives.' When the people returned, Wildcat never allowed it to be foggy any more, and he became the head chief of the village.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 196 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Grizzly-Bear and Raccoon: The Bone Needle

region.en: Alder tree by the crawfish creek (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 拾螯蝦溪畔之赤楊樹（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by Herbert J. Spinden, 1907; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Nez Perce Tales, 18. Grizzly-Bear and Raccoon'

summary.en: Little-Raccoon, sleepy after a crawfish meal, sleeps in an old crow's nest with his tail hanging over the side; Grizzly-Bear travelling the creek sees it, shakes the tree, and — told he 'backed up' — backs up the alder herself. Lying with her head back, she asks Raccoon to louse her head, but he finds no lice, only little frogs, and drops one down her ear — 'Then dig him out,' she says, giving him her long bone needle. Raccoon sets the needle in the ear and gives it a heavy blow with his fist, killing Grizzly-Bear. He roasts the meat in a pit, makes speech after speech to an imaginary crowd, eats up all the bear-meat alone, and sends his menstruating grandmother home 'lest she spoil his luck.' Angry at her treatment, the old woman puts on the hide, changes into a grizzly, pounds the ground in anger instead of camas-bread, and when Raccoon comes close catches and kills him, then goes off into the mountains.
summary.zh: 小浣熊食螯蝦後睏倦，宿於老鴉巢中，尾垂巢外。灰熊循溪而來，見其尾，搖樹而醒之；問其如何上樹，答曰『倒爬而上』——灰熊亦倒爬登樹。灰熊仰臥，命浣熊為其捉蝨；浣熊遍尋無蝨，唯見小蛙數隻，遂取一枚自其耳孔投入——『取出來！』灰熊授以長骨針。浣熊將針插入耳中，一拳猛擊，灰熊斃命。浣熊烤肉於坑，對著空氣連番演說，自稱賓客盈門，獨吞全部熊肉，並以『月事穢氣恐壞運氣』為由遣祖母回家。老嫗憤而披熊皮，化為灰熊；浣熊聞敲擊聲，誤以為祖母在搗卡瑪斯餅，近前一看，被她擒住殺死。熊遂入山而去。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Nez Perce narrative collected by Spinden (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Spinden notes Nez Perce women are carefully segregated during menstrual periods — the tale plays on that custom. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: Little-Raccoon used to hunt crawfish along the edge of the creek. One day, after catching all he could eat, he became sleepy, and climbed an alder-tree to an old crow's nest; there he went to sleep with his tail hanging over the side of the nest. Grizzly-Bear was travelling along the creek, when she happened to look up and see Raccoon's tail. So Grizzly-Bear went there, shook the tree, and woke up Raccoon. Then she said, 'How did you get up there?' and Raccoon replied, 'I backed up.' So Grizzly-Bear also backed up the tree. She said to Raccoon, 'Now, Raccoon, you may louse my head'; but the Raccoon could find no lice in the head of Grizzly-Bear, only little frogs. She was lying with her head back, and Raccoon dropped a little frog down her ear. He said to Grizzly-Bear, 'Aunt, I dropped one louse down your ear.' She replied, 'Then dig him out.' Raccoon put in his finger, but could not reach the frog; then Grizzly-Bear thought of her long bone needle, and she gave this to Raccoon to dig out the louse. Raccoon put the needle in place in the ear, and then gave it a heavy blow with his fist and killed Grizzly-Bear. Then Raccoon climbed down out of the tree, and started for home.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 196-197 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Raccoon told his grandmother that he had killed Grizzly-Bear; then they went and cut her up. Now, Raccoon's grandmother had taken off her leggings, and by chance had scratched her leg; and when Raccoon saw the blood on her leg, he said to her, 'You must go home, you are having menses.' She did not wish to go, but he compelled her to do so, lest she spoil his luck. Raccoon dug a roasting-pit, and roasted the bear-meat in it. When all was ready, he went home, and said to his grandmother, 'A large crowd has come to see me, and I do not think there will be any meat left for you.' Then he went out to the roasting-pit, where he made a fine speech and ate, and then made another fine speech and ate, until he alone had eaten up all the bear-meat; then he told his grandmother she had better take care of the hide, because that was all that was left.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 197 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: The old woman did not like the way she had been treated; so, after Raccoon had stepped outside, she put on the hide, and thus changed herself into a grizzly bear. Raccoon came back after the old woman had gone off into the brush; he could not find her around camp, so he tracked her out into the brush. Then he heard the sound of pounding, and he thought she was making camas-bread for him, but instead she was pounding the ground in anger. It was almost evening; when Raccoon called to his grandmother, 'Are you making camas-bread for me?' she replied, 'Yes!' And then, when he came close, she caught him and killed him, and then went off into the mountains.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 197 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: The Duck's Marriage: The Horn Spoons

region.en: Wedding-feast camp across the lake (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 湖彼岸喜宴之營（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by Herbert J. Spinden, 1907; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Nez Perce Tales, 19. The Duck's Marriage'

summary.en: The Mallard-Duck's son married, and the Ducks went to the wedding-feast at the camp of the bride's family, where there were fish and mussels and kaus-soup with salmon, and spoons of mountain-sheep horn with which to eat the soup. The Ducks admired these spoons very much, and when they were through eating they tucked them under their wings; they had just begun to swim across the lake when their hosts missed the spoons and called out, 'What did you do with the spoons?' 'We left them by the soup-bowl that we ate out of,' the Ducks replied — but they could not be found there, because the Ducks had already stuck them upon their noses. That is why ducks now have noses like spoons.
summary.zh: 綠頭鴨之子成婚，鴨族赴新娘家喜宴，席上有魚、蚌、卡烏斯鮭湯，並有大角羊角匙以進湯。鴨族愛不釋手，食畢藏匙於翼下；方渡湖半，主人家發覺失匙，高呼：『爾等把匙怎麼了？』鴨答：『留在湯碗旁了。』然遍尋不獲——鴨已將匙插於喙上。故今日之鴨，喙如匙狀。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Nez Perce narrative collected by Spinden (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: The Mallard-Duck's son married, and the Ducks went to the wedding-feast at the camp of the bride's family. For the feast there were fish and mussels and kaus-soup with salmon; there were spoons of mountain-sheep horn with which to eat the soup. Now, the Ducks admired these spoons very much; and when they were through eating, they tucked them under their wings. The Ducks had just begun to swim across the lake, when their hosts missed the spoons, and called out, 'What did you do with the spoons?' The Ducks replied, 'We left them by the soup-bowl that we ate out of.' They could not find the spoons there, however, because the Ducks had already stuck them upon their noses. That is why ducks now have noses like spoons.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 198 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.

title.en: The Man Who Married a Bear

region.en: Fishing camp on the Little Salmon branch of the Grande Ronde (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 格蘭德朗德河小鮭魚支流漁營（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by Herbert J. Spinden, 1907; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Nez Perce Tales, 21. The Man who married a Bear'

summary.en: A youth named Five-Times-surrounded-in-War loses himself every spring till fall, really fishing up the Little Salmon branch of the Grande Ronde; a Bear girl living below the forks of Asotin Creek circles his camp at night afraid to enter, and next evening, dressed as a human being, comes into his camp to ask whether he will marry her. He marries her and follows her home to a hole in the ground with a fine supply of winter food — then he knew she must be a bear. In the dead of winter she dreams, roars in her sleep, sings, and blood runs from her mouth: 'This blood is the blood of men; down at the mouth of Asotin Creek the hunters are making ready for a bear-hunt... five hunters are coming here.' She kills the first hunter who comes to the cave door; ten more come, and at midnight she dreams her own death — 'This blood you see coming out of my mouth is my own blood' — and at sunrise, rushing at the hung garment they have set as a decoy, she is shot when she turns to go back. The youth, recognized by the hunters, goes home with them and tells the story: this was the year before the French trappers came, and Five-Times-surrounded-in-War went away with them, returned in a year, and after that disappeared.
summary.zh: 名為五陷戰陣之少年，每年春天外出，秋深方歸，實則上格蘭德朗德河小鮭支流捕鮭。阿索廷溪匯口下有熊女，夜繞其營而不敢近；翌晚著人衣入營求婚。少年娶之，隨其歸家——竟是一地穴，冬糧豐盈——方知其為熊。隆冬之夜，熊女夢中長嘯，歌而口吐鮮血：『此乃人血。阿索廷溪口獵人正備熊獵，五人將至。』翌晨獵人果至，熊女出穴誅其一；又十人來，午夜她復夢見己死——『此血乃我自身之血』——日出之時，熊女撲向獵人所懸誘餌衣物，回身之際中彈而亡。少年出穴，獵人認出，偕歸告知此事——時在法國毛皮商東來之前一年。此後他隨商而去，一年後返回，再後音訊全無。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Nez Perce narrative collected by Spinden (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Spinden notes it is supposed to be a true tale of recent times rather than a myth; included as recorded. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: A man named Five-Times-surrounded-in-War lived with his father at Asotin, and in the spring of the year the youth would go away from home and lose himself till fall; he would tell no one where he had been. Now, he really was accustomed to go up the Little Salmon branch of the Grande Ronde River to fish for salmon; it was the second year that he went there that this thing happened. A Bear girl lived just below the forks of Asotin Creek, and from that place she used to go over on to the Little Salmon, where Five-Times-surrounded-in-War had a camp made of boughs. One day, after fishing, he was lying in his camp not quite asleep; he heard the noise of some one walking in the woods, and heard the noise of walking go all around the camp. The Grizzly-Bear girl was afraid to go near the man, and soon she went away and left him. Next morning he tried to track her; and while he could see the tracks in the grass, he could not tell what it was that made them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 198 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Next day the youth hunted deer in order to have dried meat for the winter; and that evening the Grizzly-Bear girl, dressed up as a human being, came into his camp. Five-Times-surrounded-in-War had just finished his supper when he heard the footfalls, and, looking out into the forest, he saw a fine girl come into the open. He asked the girl to tell him what she wanted, and she came and sat down beside him; the youth was bashful and could not talk to her, although she was a pretty girl. 'Where are you camping?' — she told him that three days before she had come from the forks of Asotin Creek: 'I came to see you, and to find out whether or not you would marry me.' They returned and met; and the youth fell deeply in love with the girl, and married her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 198-199 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: So they lived in his camp until she said to him, 'Now we will go to my home.' And when they arrived, he saw that she had a fine supply of winter food — dried salmon, dried meat, camas, kaus, sanitx, service-berries, and huckleberries; but what most surprised him was that they went into a hole in the ground, because then he knew she must be a bear. It grew late in the fall, and they had to stay in the cave, for the girl could not go out. In the dead of winter they were still in the cave when the snow began to settle and harden. One night, near midnight, when both were asleep in their beds, the Grizzly-Bear girl dreamed, and roared out in her sleep. She told her husband to build a fire and make a light; then the Grizzly-Bear girl sang a song, and blood came running from her mouth. She said, 'This blood you see coming from my mouth is not my blood: it is the blood of men. Down at the mouth of Asotin Creek the hunters are making ready for a bear-hunt. They have observed this cave, and five hunters are coming here to see if a bear is in it.' The Grizzly-Bear girl in her sleep knew that the hunters were making ready.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 199 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Next morning the five hunters went up to that place, and that same morning the Grizzly-Bear girl donned a different dress from what she usually wore — a dress that was painted red. She told her husband, 'Soon after the sun leaves the earth, these hunters will be here, and then I will do my killing.' They arrived, and Five-Times-surrounded-in-War heard them talking, saying that something must be living in the cave. When the first hunter came to the door of the cave, the Grizzly-Bear girl rushed out and killed him; then the four other hunters went home and told the news, and ten hunters made ready to come up and kill the bear, camping close by for the night. About midnight the Grizzly-Bear girl had another dream: she sang a song, and told her husband, 'I will leave you as soon as the sun is up. This blood you see coming out of my mouth is my own blood. The hunters are close by, and will soon be here.' Soon the youth could hear the hunters talking; then they took a pole and hung an empty garment near the mouth of the cave, and the bear rushed out at this decoy. When she turned to go back, they fired, and killed her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 200 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: The youth in the cave heard the hunters say, 'Watch out! There must be another one in the cave'; so he decided he would go out, and when he came into the light, the hunters recognized him. He went home with them and told the story. This was the year before the French trappers came, and Five-Times-surrounded-in-War went away with them; in a year he returned, and after that he disappeared.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 200 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.

region.en: Ranging grounds of the seven-headed monster (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 七首魔出沒之地（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected by Herbert J. Spinden, 1907; published 1917 (Boas & Teit)

source.work: Franz Boas and James A. Teit (eds.), Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes (1917) — 'Nez Perce Tales, 22. The Seven-Headed Monster'

summary.en: In the early days a chief who owned all kinds of property found a seven-headed monster running with his horses and cattle; it grew bigger and bigger, and the chief thought it gave him a big name, so he did not molest it — until it began to kill off the stock, then the Indians. The chief led half his band against it and all were killed but himself; then he made every effort to find a man who would win out over the monster. A poor man named Laptissa'n (Le Petit Jean, the hero of many French-Canadian tales) told the chief he would kill the monster if only the chief would furnish him a mule. Given the mule, Laptissa'n rode round and round the monster so many times that it grew weary watching and fell asleep; then Laptissa'n got down off the mule and cut the throat of the monster where the seven heads were joined into one neck.
summary.zh: 上古之世，一富庶酋長見七首魔混跡其馬牛之間，日漸壯大；酋長以為有此異獸同行可增威名，未加理會。後怪物先戮牲畜，再戮族人；酋長親率半數部眾往誅，全軍覆沒，唯其身免。於是遍訪勇者。貧漢拉普提桑（即法裔故事中之小讓 Le Petit Jean）言：『若賜我一騾，必誅此魔。』得騾之後，他繞魔騎行無數圈，魔因注視而疲，竟入睡鄉；拉普提桑下騎，就七首合一頸之處一刀割其喉。

sensitivity.note: Condensed paraphrase of a Nez Perce narrative collected by Spinden (Boas & Teit, 1917); not verbatim. Spinden identifies Laptissa'n with Le Petit Jean of French-Canadian tales. Published folk-narrative only. Category 'myth'.

passages.text: In the early days there was a chief who owned all kinds of property. He found the seven-headed monster running with his horses and cattle. This kept up for several years, and the monster grew bigger and bigger; the chief thought it gave him a big name to have such an animal running with his stock, so he did not molest it. Finally the monster began to kill off the stock; then the chief wanted to kill the monster, but he did not know just how to go about it. Then the chief thought to himself, 'To-morrow I shall take half this band of Indians, and we shall go and kill this monster.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 200 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: So they went out to kill it; but when they came in sight of the monster, and fired at it, the monster attacked in turn, and began killing the Indians. It killed all those who had gone out against it, except the chief himself. After this, the chief was afraid to attack a second time, and resigned himself to the loss of his stock; then the monster stopped killing off stock, and took to killing off Indians. It attacked the people in the village, and the chief made every effort to find a man who would win out over the monster.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, p. 200 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: Now, there was a poor man in this band named Laptissa'n. This Laptissa'n told the chief he would kill the monster if only the chief would furnish him a mule. So the chief gave him the mule, and Laptissa'n went out. He did not know exactly what to do, but he began by riding round and round the monster on the mule; finally he rode round so many times, that the monster grew weary watching, and fell asleep. Then Laptissa'n got down off the mule, and cut the throat of the monster where the seven heads were joined into one neck.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Folk-Tales of Salishan and Sahaptin Tribes, pp. 200-201 (Spinden, 1917); not verbatim.
